blurb: Fifty cats breeds in five rounds. Name the breed from its photo, its description and where it comes from.

qs.x: The Snowshoe, number 50 in the countdown. The Snowshoe takes the elegant pointed coat of the Siamese and adds a splash of white in all the right places.

qs.q: Which breed is “The werewolf cat — a patchy, masked roan that looks like it howls at the moon”?
qs.x: The Lykoi, number 49 in the countdown. The Lykoi is the cat that launched a thousand werewolf jokes, and the resemblance is uncanny.

The Chausie, number 48 in the countdown. The Chausie is one of the most genuinely wild-derived cats a person can own, a tall, long-legged athlete descended from crosses between the domestic cat and the jungle cat, Felis chaus, of Asia and the Middle East.

qs.q: Where does the Ocicat come from?
qs.x: The Ocicat, number 47 in the countdown. The Ocicat looks like a small spotted wildcat and behaves like the friendliest cat in the house.
The Toyger, number 46 in the countdown. The Toyger is exactly what its name promises, a toy tiger, a housecat deliberately bred to wear the bold vertical stripes of its giant wild cousin.
The Pixiebob, number 45 in the countdown. The Pixiebob was built to look like a wild bobcat, and it succeeds.

qs.q: Which breed is “A fishing cat from a chain of volcanic islands — stocky, wild, and built to hunt”?
qs.x: The Kurilian Bobtail, number 44 in the countdown. The Kurilian Bobtail comes from the Kuril Islands, a remote volcanic chain strung between Russia and Japan, and it carries the look of a cat shaped by hard country.
The Japanese Bobtail, number 43 in the countdown. The Japanese Bobtail is one of the oldest and most culturally loaded cats in the world.

qs.q: Where does the American Bobtail come from?
qs.x: The American Bobtail, number 42 in the countdown. The American Bobtail looks like it strolled in off a hunting trail.
The American Curl, number 41 in the countdown. The American Curl is instantly recognizable, and the giveaway is its ears.
The Donskoy (Don Sphynx), number 40 in the countdown. The Donskoy is a hairless cat with a story that begins in an act of kindness.

qs.q: Which breed is “A naked Siamese in silhouette — a slender, big-eared hairless cat from St. Petersburg”?
qs.x: The Peterbald, number 39 in the countdown. The Peterbald is what you get when a hairless cat is built on the long, fine lines of a Siamese.
The LaPerm, number 38 in the countdown. The LaPerm wears its name on its back.

qs.q: Where does the Selkirk Rex come from?
qs.x: The Selkirk Rex, number 37 in the countdown. The Selkirk Rex looks like a cat knitted out of lambswool.
The Balinese, number 36 in the countdown. The Balinese is a Siamese with a longer coat, and nothing more exotic than that.
The Havana Brown, number 35 in the countdown. The Havana Brown is one of the rarest pedigreed cats, and one of the most striking in a quiet way.

qs.q: Which breed is “The smallest of them all — a saucer-eyed sprite the size of a teacup that never sits still”?
qs.x: The Singapura, number 34 in the countdown. The Singapura is often called the smallest cat breed, and meeting one is a surprise.
The Korat, number 33 in the countdown. The Korat is one of the oldest natural cat breeds in the world, and in its native Thailand it has always meant good luck.

qs.q: Where does the Nebelung come from?
qs.x: The Nebelung, number 32 in the countdown. The Nebelung is a quiet, elegant cat in a shimmering blue-grey coat, and its name says exactly what it looks like.
The Ragamuffin, number 31 in the countdown. The Ragamuffin looks like a stuffed animal that learned to purr.
The Chartreux, number 30 in the countdown. The Chartreux is France's own blue cat, old enough to come wrapped in legend.

qs.q: Which breed is “The mink-coated middle child — a playful blend of Siamese and Burmese”?
qs.x: The Tonkinese, number 29 in the countdown. The Tonkinese sits squarely between two famous parents.
The Bombay, number 28 in the countdown. The Bombay was made to look like a wild thing and behave like a teddy bear.

qs.q: Where does the Manx come from?
qs.x: The Manx, number 27 in the countdown. The Manx is famous for what it lacks.
The Somali, number 26 in the countdown. The Somali is the Abyssinian in a flowing coat.
The Cornish Rex, number 25 in the countdown. The Cornish Rex began with a barn cat in Cornwall.

qs.q: Which breed is “The only natural spotted cat — a fast, ancient sprinter with worried eyes”?
qs.x: The Egyptian Mau, number 24 in the countdown. The Egyptian Mau looks like it stepped out of a tomb painting, and it may not be far wrong.
The Turkish Van, number 23 in the countdown. The Turkish Van earned a nickname few cats can claim.

qs.q: Where does the Turkish Angora come from?
qs.x: The Turkish Angora, number 22 in the countdown. The Turkish Angora is one of the oldest known longhaired breeds, named for Ankara, the Turkish city once called Angora.
The Savannah, number 21 in the countdown. The Savannah is the closest most people will come to keeping a wild cat.
The Munchkin, number 20 in the countdown. The Munchkin is the cat that started the dwarf-cat trend, and the arguments that came with it.

qs.q: Which breed is “A Persian in Siamese clothing — a flat-faced cloud with sapphire eyes”?
qs.x: The Himalayan, number 19 in the countdown. The Himalayan is a Persian that borrowed the Siamese coat.
The Birman, number 18 in the countdown. The Birman comes wrapped in legend.

qs.q: Where does the Burmese come from?
qs.x: The Burmese, number 17 in the countdown. The modern Burmese traces to a single cat.
The Siamese, number 16 in the countdown. Few cats are as famous as the Siamese.
The Oriental Shorthair, number 15 in the countdown. The Oriental Shorthair is what you get when you take the Siamese and open it up to every color and pattern under the sun.

qs.q: Which breed is “The living-room leopard — a glittering, athletic cat with a wild coat and a tame heart”?
qs.x: The Bengal, number 14 in the countdown. The Bengal was built to put the look of the jungle in your living room.
The Norwegian Forest Cat, number 13 in the countdown. The Norwegian Forest Cat, called the Wegie for short, is the stuff of Viking legend.

qs.q: Where does the Siberian come from?
qs.x: The Siberian, number 12 in the countdown. The Siberian is Russia's native cat and its national treasure, a hardy longhair that survived centuries of brutal winters in the forests and villages of Siberia.
The Sphynx, number 11 in the countdown. The Sphynx looks engineered in a lab, but it is an accident of nature.
The Russian Blue, number 10 in the countdown. The Russian Blue carries an air of mystery, and a likely backstory to match.

qs.q: Which breed is “The owl-eyed charmer — a sweet, folded-ear cat with a famous sit”?
qs.x: The Scottish Fold, number 9 in the countdown. The Scottish Fold began with a single barn cat.
The American Shorthair, number 8 in the countdown. The American Shorthair earned its place the hard way.

qs.q: Where does the Abyssinian come from?
qs.x: The Abyssinian, number 7 in the countdown. The Abyssinian looks like it stepped off the wall of an Egyptian tomb, and that resemblance helped build its legend.

The British Shorthair, number 6 in the countdown. The British Shorthair is the founding cat of Britain, descended from the working cats the Romans are said to have carried to the island to guard their grain.
The Devon Rex, number 5 in the countdown. The Devon Rex looks like it wandered in from a fairy tale.

qs.q: Which breed is “The Persian in pajamas — all the teddy-bear charm, half the grooming”?
qs.x: The Exotic Shorthair, number 4 in the countdown. The Exotic Shorthair is what happens when you give a Persian a wash-and-wear coat.
The Persian, number 3 in the countdown. The Persian is the cat people picture when they picture a fancy cat.

qs.q: Where does the Ragdoll come from?
qs.x: The Ragdoll, number 2 in the countdown. The Ragdoll is a modern American breed with an almost mythic origin.
The Maine Coon, number 1 in the countdown. The Maine Coon is America's own cat, and it did not come from a show ring.
